title: The 2026 M&A Report: In Search of a Wider Recovery.
gist: Global M&A value is up 15% YTD 2026 and megadeals have surpassed the 2021 record, but the recovery is narrow: small- and mid-cap deal volumes remain below norms, AI is simultaneously fueling and freezing parts of the market, and PE's stalled exit engine (33,500+ unsold portfolio companies) is choking supply for a broader rebound.

themes.theme: A two-track recovery: headline strength, narrow breadth

insights.claim: Aggregate global M&A deal value rose 15% year-over-year in the first eight months of 2026 and exceeded the 10-year average by 11%, while the number of megadeals ($10B+) hit 37, up from 24 in the same period of 2025 and above the prior cycle record of 32 set in 2021.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/jens-kengelbach
insights.so_what: The headline rebound is real but concentrated in the largest deals; investors should not read the aggregate number as broad-based market health.
insights.locator: Large-Scale M&A is Driving the Recovery

insights.claim: BCG's M&A Sentiment Index, which blends business confidence, valuation levels, interest rates and GenAI-based analysis of corporate communications, reads 83 as of 2026 (up from 79 at the start of the year) but remains well below its long-term average of 100.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/jens-kengelbach
insights.so_what: Sentiment improving but still depressed suggests dealmakers should expect continued caution rather than a full-throttle boom in 2026.

insights.claim: The constraint on M&A has shifted from buyer appetite and available capital toward execution: whether enough attractive opportunities can clear the economic, operational, and regulatory hurdles between intention and closing.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/jens-kengelbach
insights.so_what: Dealmakers and advisors should focus resources on deal-execution capability (diligence, structuring, regulatory navigation) rather than on capital-raising or sentiment-building.
insights.quote: The constraints on dealmaking are shifting from buyer appetite and available capital to execution.

insights.claim: Despite improving conditions, several structural headwinds persist: valuation gaps between buyers and sellers, scarcity of attractive assets, and AI-driven uncertainty about business models and future performance make many deals hard to justify even though capital and financing are available.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/jens-kengelbach
insights.so_what: Capital availability alone won't unlock the market; watch valuation-gap and asset-quality indicators as the real bottleneck to track.

themes.theme: The missing middle: small and mid-cap deals lag, and conviction is as scarce as assets

insights.claim: Deals valued at $250 million to $1 billion, and even more so those under $250 million, remain below their longer-term average deal-volume norms, and because the figures are not inflation-adjusted the real shortfall in smaller transactions is even more pronounced than reported.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/jens-kengelbach
insights.so_what: Sub-$1B deal flow is the real recovery signal to watch; a jump there, not more megadeals, would confirm the market has truly turned.

insights.claim: 27 of the year's 37 megadeals involved a buyer, target, or both located in the US, showing that the largest-deal boom is disproportionately a US phenomenon rather than a globally broad-based trend.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/jens-kengelbach
insights.so_what: US megacap exposure explains most of the reported global M&A strength; non-US large-cap deal flow is comparatively weak.

insights.claim: The market is bifurcating not just on deal size but on asset quality and conviction: buyers compete aggressively where they can underwrite growth, competitive advantage and cash generation, but assets with uncertain business models or seller expectations resting on too many assumptions struggle to generate competitive tension or clear at acceptable valuations — a 'missing middle' of conviction compounding the 'missing middle' of assets.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/jens-kengelbach
insights.so_what: Sellers should prioritize asset preparation and narrative clarity over timing the market; well-prepared, high-conviction assets can still command strong competition even in a selective market.
insights.quote: a “missing middle” of conviction is compounding the “missing middle” of assets

insights.claim: Cautious selectivity in the current market favors strategic (corporate) buyers over financial buyers, because a corporate acquirer that can underwrite buyer-specific cost, revenue, or capital synergies can pay more than a financial buyer relying on a standalone investment case — an advantage that is especially decisive for mature sponsor-owned assets held beyond their typical exit window.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/jens-kengelbach
insights.so_what: Strategic acquirers have a relative pricing edge right now on stuck, aged PE assets; PE sellers may need to accept lower multiples or wait for financial-buyer conditions to improve.

insights.claim: North America accounted for more than half of aggregate global M&A deal value in the first eight months of 2026, with North American targets totaling $1.2 trillion (+17% YoY) and US targets alone at $1.1 trillion, representing 54% of overall global M&A activity.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/jens-kengelbach
insights.so_what: The US remains the center of gravity for global deal value; regional M&A strategies should weight US exposure heavily.

insights.claim: European M&A value totaled $541 billion, up 43% YoY, led by the UK (+85% to $178 billion), Germany (+149%), Ireland (+127%), Netherlands (+79%), France (+27%) and Spain (+19%), while Switzerland (-36%), the Nordics (-15%) and Italy (-7%) declined.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/jens-kengelbach
insights.so_what: Europe posted the strongest percentage growth of any region, but the growth is highly concentrated in the UK, Germany and Ireland, not evenly spread across the continent.

insights.claim: Asia-Pacific deal value fell 27% to $245 billion, dragged down by declines in mainland China (-55%), Japan (-44%), South Korea (-23%) and India (-13%), even as Malaysia (+300%), Indonesia (+105%), Singapore (+79%), Hong Kong (+23%) and Taiwan (+18%) posted strong gains.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/jens-kengelbach
insights.so_what: APAC M&A strength is rotating away from China/Japan/Korea toward Southeast Asia; deal-sourcing strategies in the region should adjust accordingly.

insights.claim: By sector, health care (+74%) and materials (+44%) posted the largest M&A value increases; consumer goods (+20%), energy (+16%), TMT (+11%, still the largest sector by aggregate value) and financial institutions/real estate (+12%) also grew, while industrials was the only sector to decline, down 20% after being a strong performer a year earlier.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/jens-kengelbach
insights.so_what: Health care and materials are the standout sector rotations for 2026 deal flow; industrials is the notable laggard reversing from prior-year strength.

insights.claim: South and Central American M&A value fell 22% back to average levels after 2025 activity was artificially inflated by an announced-then-withdrawn transaction involving Panama Ports Company and CK Hutchison's non-Chinese port assets; Africa, the Middle East and Central Asia saw deal value rise 102% but remained well below 2019 and 2021 peaks.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/jens-kengelbach
insights.so_what: The prior year's South/Central America M&A spike was a one-off distortion from a withdrawn CK Hutchison ports deal, not underlying market strength — a caution against overreading single-deal-driven regional figures.

themes.theme: AI as a double-edged sword in dealmaking

insights.claim: AI simultaneously fuels M&A activity — encouraging investment within the AI ecosystem and among non-AI companies acquiring AI capabilities — and injects new uncertainty into the durability of business models, revenue pools, competitive positions and cost structures for assets exposed to AI-driven disruption.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/jens-kengelbach
insights.so_what: Investors should treat 'AI exposure' as a two-sided variable in deal underwriting — it can be an acquisition driver or a valuation depressant depending on whether the target is an AI beneficiary or an AI-disruption target.
insights.quote: AI is becoming a double-edged sword in M&A.
insights.locator: AI is fueling M&A but also making some deals harder

insights.claim: Technology sector M&A sentiment is the weakest of all sectors tracked at 52 (versus financial institutions at 108, health care at 100, and energy/utilities at 96), even though technology, media and telecommunications leads all sectors in aggregate deal value — reflecting scrutiny of software business models exposed to AI disruption even as AI-native assets attract strong demand.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/jens-kengelbach
insights.so_what: High tech deal value but low tech sentiment is a red flag: dealmakers are transacting in tech out of necessity/opportunity, not confidence — expect more deal breakage or repricing in software M&A.

insights.claim: The sharp correction in software-company valuations earlier in 2026, combined with a decline in PE deal activity in software, is cited as early evidence that AI-driven uncertainty is making parts of the existing software asset universe harder to price and harder to transact.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/jens-kengelbach
insights.so_what: The 2026 software valuation correction is framed as an AI-disruption effect, not a generic multiple compression — investors in software M&A should price in AI-obsolescence risk explicitly.
insights.locator: AI is fueling M&A but also making some deals harder

insights.claim: Venture capital remains heavily concentrated in AI, attracting capital at a pace the report describes as reminiscent of previous technology booms.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/jens-kengelbach
insights.so_what: An implicit bubble-parallel warning: VC funding concentration in AI at boom-like pace is a signal to watch for overvaluation risk in AI-native private assets.
insights.quote: Venture capital, meanwhile, remains heavily concentrated in AI, which is attracting capital at a pace reminiscent of previous technology booms.

insights.claim: In AI dealmaking specifically, companies are increasingly using a modular approach that combines equity stakes with partnerships and contractual rights rather than relying solely on conventional full-control acquisitions.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/jens-kengelbach
insights.so_what: Expect more AI deals structured as minority stakes, partnerships and contractual rights rather than outright acquisitions — a template for navigating valuation and technology uncertainty.
insights.locator: Alternative deal structures can bridge uncertainty

themes.theme: Private equity's stalled exit engine is choking deal supply

insights.claim: PE firms held more than 33,500 unsold portfolio companies as of June 30, 2026, up from about 32,500 at the end of 2025 and more than double the level of a decade ago, according to PitchBook data.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/jens-kengelbach
insights.so_what: A record backlog of unsold PE companies is a large, quantifiable overhang of future deal supply — a key leading indicator for M&A volume once exit conditions improve.

insights.claim: Median PE holding periods have stretched materially: US portfolio companies sold in 2025 had a median holding period of 5.3 years, up from 4.3 years for those sold in 2020 (Gain.AI); in Europe median holding periods rose from about 4.6 to 5.8 years over the same period, and roughly one-third of PE-owned assets have now been held more than seven years.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/jens-kengelbach
insights.so_what: Extended holding periods signal a large cohort of aging PE assets that will eventually need to transact, creating a potential supply wave for buyers patient enough to wait out the current valuation-gap standoff.

insights.claim: PE's buy-hold-exit-reinvest capital-recycling engine is not running at full speed; sponsors need to exit more portfolio companies and return more capital to limited partners for PE to contribute more extensively to a broader M&A recovery, and this backlog of mature sponsor-owned assets is holding back an important source of transaction supply for the whole market.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/jens-kengelbach
insights.so_what: PE exit velocity, not fundraising or dry powder, is the binding constraint on M&A supply — LPs and PE-fund investors should watch distribution rates as the key leading signal for market breadth.

insights.claim: Sponsor-backed M&A deal value grew 11% in the first eight months of 2026, driven by stronger PE activity in Europe and North America, even as concerns about stress in private credit markets and the outlook for software-heavy portfolios continue to weigh on the sector.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/jens-kengelbach
insights.so_what: PE dealmaking is recovering but remains shadowed by private-credit stress and software-portfolio concerns — a risk to monitor for sponsor-backed deal financing conditions.

themes.theme: Regulatory risk is relocating, not disappearing

insights.claim: Conventional antitrust scrutiny has eased in parts of the market, with regulators blocking fewer transactions and making greater use of conditional approvals and remedies, resulting in fewer abandoned deals — but the regulatory burden has shifted rather than vanished, toward national security screening, industrial policy, foreign investment controls, and foreign subsidy reviews.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/jens-kengelbach
insights.so_what: Don't read looser antitrust enforcement as a broad regulatory tailwind — cross-border and strategically sensitive deals now face a different, possibly more unpredictable, set of national-security and subsidy-review hurdles.
insights.quote: Regulatory risk is shifting rather than receding.
insights.locator: Regulatory risk is shifting rather than receding

insights.claim: The European Commission is revising its merger guidelines to place greater emphasis on competitiveness, resilience, innovation and efficiencies, while the EU Foreign Subsidies Regulation has added another layer of scrutiny for qualifying transactions.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/jens-kengelbach
insights.so_what: Cross-border deals into the EU should budget for an additional foreign-subsidy review layer alongside traditional merger control, extending timelines and diligence scope.
insights.locator: Regulatory risk is shifting rather than receding

insights.claim: Regulatory executability doesn't depend only on whether a deal can ultimately secure approval — the time required, and the remedies and commitments imposed, can affect the deal's economics and in some cases determine whether the original deal thesis still holds.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/jens-kengelbach
insights.so_what: Dealmakers should model regulatory timeline and remedy risk as a direct input to deal economics and thesis viability, not just as a binary go/no-go approval risk.
insights.locator: Regulatory risk is shifting rather than receding

themes.theme: The five gates: a framework for deal executability

insights.claim: BCG proposes five gates that determine whether a transaction is executable: Asset Availability and Readiness, Economics and Market Clearing, Financial Resilience, Organizational Capacity, and Regulatory Clearance.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/jens-kengelbach
insights.so_what: A practical due-diligence checklist for dealmakers to pressure-test any transaction before committing resources — asset readiness and price agreement should be scrutinized first.
insights.quote: Five gates determine whether a transaction is executable
insights.locator: Factors That Will Shape the Next Phase of the M&A Cycle

insights.claim: Asset availability and economics (price/value agreement) are currently the most important constraints on a broader M&A recovery, regulatory complexity is a particularly important test for large and cross-border deals, while financing and organizational capacity are less constraining at the market level today, though they can still sink individual deals.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/jens-kengelbach
insights.so_what: Capital and org-capacity are not the bottleneck right now — deal teams should focus scarce effort on sourcing ready assets and closing valuation gaps rather than on financing structuring.
insights.locator: Factors That Will Shape the Next Phase of the M&A Cycle

insights.claim: Dealmakers should test all five executability gates as part of the deal thesis itself upfront, rather than addressing them sequentially only after a preferred transaction has already emerged.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/jens-kengelbach
insights.so_what: A process recommendation: front-load regulatory, financing and organizational-capacity assessment into initial deal screening to avoid late-stage deal failure.
insights.locator: Factors That Will Shape the Next Phase of the M&A Cycle

themes.theme: Paths to a broader recovery: portfolio rotation and flexible deal structures

insights.claim: Portfolio rotation — corporate divestitures of mature, noncore businesses plus PE exits — is identified as the most likely mechanism to broaden the M&A recovery, because the binding constraint is supply (asset readiness), not demand.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/jens-kengelbach
insights.so_what: Watch corporate divestiture announcements and PE exit rates as the leading indicators of a genuinely broadening M&A cycle, more than aggregate deal-value headlines.
insights.quote: Portfolio rotation can broaden the recovery.
insights.locator: Portfolio rotation can broaden the recovery

insights.claim: Lazard's analysis of shareholder activism in the first half of 2026 identifies M&A and capital allocation as the most prevalent activist campaign objectives, indicating rising external pressure on companies to revisit their portfolio choices.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/jens-kengelbach
insights.so_what: Activist investors are a rising catalyst pushing corporates toward divestitures and portfolio M&A — a signal for which companies may face forced asset sales.
insights.locator: Portfolio rotation can broaden the recovery

insights.claim: Alternative deal structures — minority investments, joint ventures, staged acquisitions, earnouts, and rollover equity — let buyers and sellers share risks around valuation, control, regulation and technology, rather than forcing a binary choice between 100% acquisition and no transaction; different structures solve different problems (earnouts/rollover equity bridge valuation gaps, minority stakes/JVs give strategic access without control, staged deals preserve optionality).
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/jens-kengelbach
insights.so_what: Dealmakers facing valuation-gap standoffs should reach for structured/partial deal formats rather than walking away — this is a practical playbook for closing deals in an uncertain environment.
insights.locator: Alternative deal structures can bridge uncertainty

insights.claim: Competition for scarce, high-quality assets could push their valuations even higher even as less attractive businesses struggle to find buyers at all, heightening the importance of distinguishing genuine strategic conviction from market exuberance.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/jens-kengelbach
insights.so_what: Expect a widening valuation bifurcation between top-quality and lesser assets rather than a market-wide multiple convergence — a caution against chasing scarce 'trophy' assets at any price.

insights.claim: As deal activity accelerates, competitive advantage in the next phase of M&A will belong not to those with the most capital or the greatest appetite for deals, but to those that can identify the right opportunities, structure deals for success, and actually deliver the value they envisioned.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/jens-kengelbach
insights.so_what: Capital access is no longer a differentiator among dealmakers; execution skill (sourcing, structuring, post-deal value delivery) is the new competitive edge to underwrite when evaluating acquirers.
insights.quote: Advantage in the next phase of M&A may therefore belong not to those with the most capital or the greatest appetite for deals, but to those that can identify the right opportunities, structure deals for success, and deliver the value they envisioned.
